title: Episode 137: James Buchanan and the Dred Scott Firestorm: The Bachelor in the White House
description:
James Buchanan of Pennsylvania entered the White House in March eighteen fifty-seven possessing perhaps the most impressive diplomatic and legislative resume in American history. He had served forty years in public office: as a state legislator, congressman, minister to Russia, United States senator, Secretary of State under James K. Polk, and minister to Great Britain. He was also unique in presidential history: tall, distinguished, blind in one eye with a peculiar tilted head posture, Buchanan was—and remains to this day—the only lifelong bachelor to occupy the presidency.

Convinced that his vast diplomatic seasoning gave him the wisdom to calm sectional strife, Buchanan committed an act of shocking unconstitutional meddling before he even took the oath. During the winter of eighteen fifty-seven, Buchanan secretly corresponded with two Supreme Court justices, lobbying fellow Pennsylvanian Justice Robert Grier to join the Southern majority in the pending freedom suit of an enslaved man named Dred Scott. Buchanan wanted a sweeping decision that would ban Congress from ever restricting slavery in territories, falsely believing it would settle the issue forever.

At his inauguration, Buchanan hypocritically announced that the Supreme Court was about to rule on the slavery question, promising that he would cheerfully submit to its authority. Two days later, Chief Justice Roger B. Taney delivered the catastrophic Dred Scott decision, ruling that Black Americans were not citizens and 'had no rights which the white man was bound to respect.' Rather than pacifying the country, Buchanan's judicial conspiracy detonated a firestorm of Northern fury and propelled Abraham Lincoln to national prominence. Here is George with the full story.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the presidency of our fifteenth chief executive, James Buchanan. Buchanan was widely considered the most qualified man to ever hold the office, having served as a senator, secretary of state, and ambassador across Europe. He was also our only bachelor president. Yet behind his polished manners lay a catastrophic vanity. In eighteen fifty-seven, Buchanan secretly colluded with the Supreme Court to settle the slavery question once and for all, triggering the darkest judicial ruling in American history: the Dred Scott decision. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE BACHELOR OF WHEATLAND
In the autumn of eighteen fifty-six, James Buchanan of Pennsylvania seemed like the providential answer to a divided nation's prayers. At age sixty-five, Buchanan possessed an extraordinary resume: forty years of unblemished public service as a state representative, five terms in Congress, minister to Czarist Russia, ten years in the Senate, Secretary of State under James K. Polk, and minister to Great Britain. Because he had been living in London during the bloody debates over the Kansas-Nebraska Act, Buchanan was completely untainted by the violence of Bleeding Kansas, making him the ideal compromise nominee for the Democratic Party.
Buchanan was physically imposing and distinctive: tall, broad-shouldered, impeccably groomed, with a heavy shock of white hair. Because he suffered from an eye defect that left one eye farsighted and the other nearsighted, he walked with a peculiar, gentle tilt of his head to one side, giving him an air of perpetual, courtly attentiveness. He was also unique in the annals of the American presidency: Buchanan was, and remains to this day, the only lifelong bachelor ever elected President of the United States.
In his youth, Buchanan had been engaged to a wealthy young woman named Ann Coleman. But following a tragic misunderstanding fueled by town gossip, Coleman broke off the engagement in eighteen nineteen and died days later of an accidental laudanum overdose. Grief-stricken, Buchanan vowed never to marry, retreating into a quiet, solitary personal life at his country estate of Wheatland near Lancaster, Pennsylvania. In eighteen fifty-six, Buchanan won the presidency, promising to use his vast diplomatic mastery to restore harmony to the republic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE ENSLAVED TRAVELER: DRED SCOTT
While Buchanan was preparing for his inauguration, a modest legal case that had wound through state and federal courts for eleven years was reaching its climax before the United States Supreme Court. The case centered on a humble, illiterate enslaved man named Dred Scott.
Born into slavery in Virginia around seventeen ninety-nine, Scott had been purchased in eighteen thirty-three by an army surgeon named Dr. John Emerson. Over the next decade, Emerson took Scott with him to various military duty stations, living for several years at Fort Armstrong in Illinois, where slavery was prohibited by state constitution, and at Fort Snelling in the Wisconsin Territory—modern-day Minnesota—where slavery was strictly banned by the Missouri Compromise of eighteen twenty. At Fort Snelling, Scott married an enslaved woman named Harriet Robinson, and they had two daughters.
Following Dr. Emerson's death, Scott returned to Missouri. In eighteen forty-six, backed by abolitionist lawyers and his former owners' family, Scott filed a formal freedom suit in the St. Louis circuit court. He cited the long-standing legal doctrine of 'once free, always free'—arguing that by residing in free states and territories where slavery was prohibited by federal law, he and his family had lawfully acquired their freedom. Lower Missouri courts agreed and declared Scott free, but pro-slavery appeals pushed the case all the way to the United States Supreme Court.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SECRET COLLUSION IN THE ROBING ROOM
By early eighteen fifty-seven, the Supreme Court was deeply divided. Seven of the nine justices were Democrats, and five, including eighty-year-old Chief Justice Roger B. Taney of Maryland, were from slaveholding Southern states. Initially, the court intended to issue a narrow ruling based on Missouri state law without addressing the broader constitutional status of slavery in federal territories.
Enter President-elect James Buchanan. In an act of shocking, unprecedented unconstitutional interference, Buchanan crossed the sacrosanct boundary separating the executive and judicial branches. Believing that a definitive Supreme Court ruling could crush the rising Republican Party and eliminate slavery as a national political issue forever, Buchanan began secretly writing confidential letters to Supreme Court justices.
Buchanan wrote to Justice John Catron of Tennessee, asking when the decision would be announced and urging a broad, sweeping ruling. Learning that the five Southern justices were prepared to rule the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional, Buchanan feared that a five-to-four sectional decision along the Mason-Dixon line would look like naked Southern tyranny. Buchanan personally lobbied fellow Pennsylvania Justice Robert Grier, writing an impassioned private letter pressuring Grier to break with the Northern justices and join the Southern majority. Grier capitulated, providing Buchanan with the broad, bipartisan cover he craved.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE HYPOCRITICAL PORTICO
On March fourth, eighteen fifty-seven, James Buchanan stood on the east portico of the Capitol to take the oath of office as the fifteenth President. Spectators in the crowd noticed that just moments before taking the oath, Buchanan leaned down and engaged in a brief, animated whisper with Chief Justice Roger B. Taney.
Moments later, Buchanan stepped to the podium and delivered one of the most hypocritical, dishonest inaugural addresses in American history. Addressing the explosive question of slavery in the territories, Buchanan calmly dismissed it as a matter of minor significance that was about to be peacefully and permanently settled.
Buchanan looked out at the assembled thousands and said with smooth, pious innocence: 'A difference of opinion has arisen in regard to the point of time when the people of a Territory shall decide this question for themselves. This is, happily, a matter of but little practical importance. Besides, it is a judicial question, which legitimately belongs to the Supreme Court of the United States, before whom it is now pending, and will, it is understood, be speedily and finally settled. To their decision, in common with all good citizens, I shall cheerfully submit, whatever this may be.'
Buchanan spoke as if he were an impartial spectator humbly awaiting divine judicial guidance, completely concealing from the American people that he had secretly engineered the verdict in the judges' private conference room.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: TANEY'S DARK DECREE: MARCH 6, 1857
Two days later, on Friday, March sixth, eighteen fifty-seven, Chief Justice Roger Brooke Taney entered the Supreme Court chamber to read the majority opinion in Scott versus Sandford. Emaciated, eighty years old, with hollow cheeks and claw-like hands, Taney spoke for two hours in a voice that was barely more than a dry, rasping whisper, but his words shook the foundations of the American republic.
Taney's opinion went far beyond Dred Scott's personal freedom. First, Taney declared that no Black person—whether enslaved or free—could ever be a citizen of the United States or sue in federal court. Sifting through colonial statutes, Taney asserted that the framers of the Constitution had regarded Black people as 'beings of an inferior order, and altogether unfit to associate with the white race, either in social or political relations; and so far inferior, that they had no rights which the white man was bound to respect.'
Second, Taney struck down the Missouri Compromise of eighteen twenty as unconstitutional—marking only the second time in American history that the Supreme Court had invalidated an act of Congress. Taney ruled that under the Fifth Amendment, enslaved people were private property, and that Congress possessed no constitutional authority to deprive citizens of their property anywhere in the federal territories. Therefore, any federal law prohibiting slavery anywhere in the United States was void. By Taney's decree, slavery was nationalized across the entire continent.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE NORTHERN EXPLOSION
James Buchanan and Roger Taney had intended to kill the anti-slavery movement with a single judicial blow. Instead, the Dred Scott decision detonated an explosion of Northern rage unlike anything seen since the Boston Tea Party. Northern newspapers denounced Taney's opinion as an abomination, a wicked perversion of the Constitution, and an insult to human civilization.
Northern state legislatures passed resolutions declaring the decision non-binding. Frederick Douglass, the great Black abolitionist orator, delivered a thunderous speech declaring: 'My hopes were never brighter than now. This very attempt to blot out forever the hopes of an enslaved people may be one necessary link in the chain of events preparatory to the downfall and complete overthrow of the whole slave system.'
In Illinois, a lanky country lawyer named Abraham Lincoln was galvanized out of semi-retirement. Lincoln systematically dismantled Taney's historical falsehoods, pointing out that in five of the original thirteen states, free Black men had voted to ratify the United States Constitution. Lincoln pointed his finger directly at the suspicious whisper between Buchanan and Taney on the inauguration portico. In his immortal 'House Divided' speech in eighteen fifty-eight, Lincoln openly accused 'Stephen, Franklin, Roger, and James'—Stephen Douglas, Franklin Pierce, Roger Taney, and James Buchanan—of operating as a coordinated architectural conspiracy to nationalize slavery and transform the United States into a slave empire.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE VERDICT ON BUCHANAN'S FOLLY
James Buchanan's secret judicial meddling proved to be the supreme catastrophic blunder of the antebellum era. By attempting to short-circuit the democratic political process and impose a pro-slavery judicial fiat upon a protesting majority, Buchanan destroyed the legitimacy of the Supreme Court, shattered the Northern wing of the Democratic Party, and made civil war virtually inevitable.
When Dred Scott was declared a slave by the highest court in the land, a bitter irony followed: two months after the ruling, Scott's original owners, the Sons of Peter Blow, purchased Dred Scott and his family from his Southern masters and formally signed his emancipation papers in a St. Louis courtroom. Dred Scott spent the final year of his life as a free man, working as a hotel porter in St. Louis before dying of tuberculosis in September eighteen fifty-eight.
For James Buchanan, the Dred Scott ruling was the beginning of an unmitigated disaster. Having embraced the Southern radical doctrine, Buchanan proceeded to back the fraudulent Lecompton Constitution in Kansas, alienating Stephen Douglas and tearing the Democratic Party in two. By eighteen sixty, the party was fractured, paving the way for Abraham Lincoln's election and the collapse of the Union.
James Buchanan had believed that political cunning, backroom collusion, and diplomatic maneuvering could outwit the moral conscience of a free people. He learned too late that when a government uses the law to strip human beings of their God-given rights, it does not preserve peace—it unleashes the whirlwind.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
James Buchanan's collusion in the Dred Scott decision proved that backroom judicial maneuvering cannot silence the moral conscience of a nation. Next week, we turn to James Buchanan's final, tragic chapter: the Winter of Secession in eighteen hundred and sixty, where as state after state tore itself from the Union, the paralyzed President sat in the White House counting the days until he could hand a shattered republic to Abraham Lincoln. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
